title: Blue Cross Analysis Links AI Coding Tools to $942 Million In Added Healthcare Spending
source_used: Yahoo (rewrite crediting Quartz), Chief Healthcare Executive and Outsource Accelerator; Telehealth.org and Quartz pages return 403
key_facts: The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA) analysis estimates AI-enabled hospital coding added about $942 million to spending for Blue Cross and Blue Shield companies from 2023 to 2025.
More than 60% of hospital systems now use AI tools to scan lab results and records for secondary diagnoses; about 70% of the added spending, over $650 million, came from secondary diagnoses.
The data are de-identified claims from member companies covering one in three Americans, centred on inpatient care.
In major bowel procedures, diagnoses such as partial intestinal blockages rose 55% and acid overload 33% between Q1 2023 and Q4 2025 while treatment rates stayed flat.
Complex cases rose from 37% of cases in 2023 to 40% in late 2025.

The American Hospital Association (AHA) rejects the finding: BCBSA did not review medical records or identify which claims involved AI, and sicker, older inpatients explain more complex coding; the AHA estimates coding intensity added about 0.3 points to commercial spending growth.
Our own editions carried the analysis on 25 and 27 Sep 2026 and the AHA reply on 6 Oct 2026; other coverage: Newscord 27 Sep, Quartz 28 Sep, CNBC 1 Oct; the Telehealth.org item is dated 16 Oct.
quote_evidence: A new Blue Cross Blue Shield Association analysis suggests artificial intelligence billing software may be pushing up hospital costs even when patients are not actually sicker and their treatment is no more intensive.
The association said the tools increased healthcare spending for Blue Cross and Blue Shield companies by an estimated $942 million from 2023 to 2025, according to Quartz.
The AHA argues that BCBSA largely attributed rising patient complexity to coding behavior while overlooking well-documented changes in who ends up in hospital beds.
why_it_matters_hint: Insurers say AI coding raised costs; hospitals say the patients are sicker and the proof is missing.
event_date: BCBSA analysis carried in our 25 and 27 Sep 2026 editions; AHA reply 5 Oct 2026 (our 6 Oct edition).
